data.text/markdown:
Can we predict who comes back to the hospital?

CAI 5735 Final Project - Ryan Merlino, [MEMBER 2], [MEMBER 3]

Research question

How accurately can a diabetes patient's length of stay, number of lab tests, procedures, medications and diagnoses, plus whether they were prescribed a diabetes medication, predict whether they will be readmitted to the hospital?
The problem. Hospitals try to prevent avoidable readmissions, which are bad for patients and costly (US hospitals are financially penalised for excess readmissions). If a model could flag high-risk patients before discharge, staff could focus follow-up calls, medication reviews and home care on them. We test how far a few simple numbers recorded during the stay can take us.

The dataset

Source: Diabetes 130-US Hospitals for Years 1999-2008, UCI Machine Learning Repository. Strack et al. (2014), Impact of HbA1c measurement on hospital readmission rates, BioMed Research International. https://doi.org/10.24432/C5230J. Our copy is a simplified 3,000-stay sample (from 130 hospitals) supplied by the course.
Column Role Meaning
readmitted Response Came back to the hospital? (we use: yes / no)
time_in_hospital Predictor Days in hospital
num_lab_procedures Predictor Lab tests during the stay
num_procedures Predictor Non-lab procedures
num_medications Predictor Distinct medications given
number_diagnoses Predictor Diagnoses recorded
diabetes_med Predictor Prescribed a diabetes medication (yes / no)
age, gender, admission_type Not used Left out to focus on in-stay measurements

The original outcome has three levels: not readmitted (1799), after 30 days (920), within 30 days (281). Because our question is whether a patient returns, we merge the last two into readmitted (1201 stays, 40%). No values are missing.

Explore the data

Pick a variable to see how its distribution differs between readmitted and not-readmitted stays. The differences are small, which already hints at the result.

data.text/markdown:
Analysis process

  1. Split: 75% training / 25% test (stratified, random_state=42). Every number below comes from the 750 held-out test stays.
  2. Three models: logistic regression (interpretable baseline), a depth-4 decision tree, and a random forest of trees.
  3. Evaluate each with a confusion matrix, accuracy, sensitivity (share of real readmissions caught), specificity (share of non-readmissions correctly cleared), and the ROC curve / AUROC.
Use the controls to explore a model and threshold. The threshold is the predicted probability above which we label a patient "readmitted".

Model comparison (test set, threshold 0.5)

Model Accuracy Sensitivity Specificity AUROC
Logistic regression 0.583 0.157 0.867 0.587
Decision tree 0.604 0.300 0.807 0.586
Random forest 0.613 0.213 0.880 0.588
Which is best? The random forest has the top AUROC and accuracy, so it is our pick, but the three models are nearly tied (AUROC about 0.59). Logistic regression is a reasonable alternative because it is simpler to explain. At 0.5 every model has very low sensitivity: they mostly guess "not readmitted", and 60% of stays are not readmitted, so 60% accuracy is the baseline to beat. Threshold. Missing a patient who comes back is worse than an unnecessary follow-up call, so we want higher sensitivity. For the random forest, 0.40 maximises Youden's J (sensitivity 0.66, specificity 0.48). Drag the slider to see the trade-off: below about 0.35 almost every patient is flagged, and above 0.5 almost nobody is.

Try it: classify a new patient

Enter a patient's stay details and see each model's predicted chance of readmission.

Model P(readmitted) Prediction at threshold 0.40
Logistic regression 46% Readmitted
Decision tree 54% Readmitted
Random forest 51% Readmitted

Results and conclusion

Answer: not very accurately. With these six variables, our best model (random forest) reaches an AUROC of about 0.59, where 0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect. Its 61% accuracy at threshold 0.5 barely beats always predicting "not readmitted" (60%). Lowering the threshold to 0.40 catches about two-thirds of readmissions, but only by wrongly flagging about half of the patients who do not return. What this means. Counts recorded during the stay (days, tests, medications) are only weakly related to coming back. Better predictors probably include prior admissions, discharge destination and lab results like HbA1c, none of which are in this simplified file. As it stands, the model could be a rough screening aid, but it should not drive decisions about individual patients. Limitations. A 3,000-row sample, one random split (results vary by about +/- 0.02 AUROC), no tuning of hyperparameters, and data from 1999-2008.
